claims_disputed.claim: Programmers accept correct assertions far more reliably than they reject incorrect ones, with similar confidence in both.
claims_disputed.reason: The asymmetry is statistically clear (73.9% vs 49.0%, OR 2.94, §6.1), but §4 says RQ1 was not pre-registered; it emerged from early analysis. It rests on one corpus of 26 HumanEval functions with one incorrect GPT-3.5-era postcondition each, filtered to be plausible (§3.1.2). Fig. 5 shows the effect is stimulus-dependent: 'common' gives 92% vs 10%, but 'match_parens' reverses (incorrect detected 82.4%, correct accepted 18.2%). Participants could not execute the assertions. A post hoc finding on a single small stimulus set is moderate, not strong.

claims_disputed.claim: Assertion completeness is only weakly related to judgement accuracy.
claims_disputed.reason: §6.3 reports Spearman rho=0.18 between participants' completeness RATINGS and the mutation-based bug-completeness score, not between completeness and judgement accuracy. The paper reads it as developers being able to tell stronger from weaker specifications. No analysis of completeness against accuracy is reported, so the claim as worded has no evidence.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: No approval gate is compared with an alternative (an automated check, execution, or no gate). The paper measures human judgement accuracy on its own, and the correct-vs-incorrect split is a property of the stimuli, not an isolating comparison of the pattern. The 49% detection rate belongs in a contribution, not a stance.

missed_issues: Judgements were read-only in an online survey; participants could not run the assertion on inputs. The think-aloud shows negative examples were the main way to confirm suspected errors (18/29, §6.4), so the obvious mitigation, executing the oracle against counterexamples, was never tested. The 49% applies to review by reading.
Fig. 5 is internally inconsistent: the choose_num row reports 0.6 and 0.611 with a difference of 1.1, mixing proportion and percent scales.
The paper disagrees with itself on the generator: §3.1.2 says Endres et al. generated postconditions with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, while §9 says the postconditions were generated by GPT-3.5.

Think-aloud coding reliability is not reported: two authors jointly coded one transcript, then the first author alone coded the other nine (§4.2). The five strategies and the 'intuition is usually wrong' (7/12) observation are single-coder.

Low discrimination may be partly response bias: accepting 74% of correct and 51% of incorrect assertions is consistent with a general 'looks fine' tendency, which the paper does not separate from sensitivity.
note: I agree with the P41 'contradicts' stance (explanation vs no explanation is a pre-registered isolating comparison and explanations did not help), the verdict and the weak grades on the explanation-harm and 'AI assistance' claims. I lower the headline asymmetry to moderate because it is exploratory, comes from one 26-function GPT-3.5 corpus, reverses for some functions and excludes execution. The completeness claim misreads §6.3 and is unsupported. P19 'mixed' has no comparison behind it. I score rigor and relevance one point lower than the review; it is a careful human study, but on toy Python with read-only review.
